title: Book 8 — Urania, Chapter 87
paragraphs: As for the rest, I cannot speak of them individually or say precisely how the barbarians or Greeks fought each on their own. But with regard to Artemisia, this is what happened, by which she gained even more esteem from the king than before. When the king's affairs had fallen into great confusion, at that crisis a ship of Artemisia was being pursued by an Athenian ship; unable to escape (since ahead of her lay other ships of her own side, while her own ship happened to be the most advanced toward the enemy), she decided what to do, and it proved greatly to her advantage that she did. Being pursued by the Athenian ship, she charged at full speed into a ship of her own side manned by Calyndians, with the king of the Calyndians, Damasithymos, aboard. Now even if it be true that she had had some quarrel with him earlier, while still at the Hellespont, I cannot say whether she did this by design, or whether the Calyndian ship happened by chance to fall in her way. Having rammed it and sunk it, she enjoyed good fortune and gained benefit two ways over. First, the Athenian captain, when he saw her ram a ship manned by barbarians, turned away and went after others, supposing Artemisia's ship was either a Greek vessel, or a deserter from the barbarians fighting for the Greeks.

First, I say, it was her good fortune to escape and not be destroyed. Secondly, though she had done harm, she yet gained great reputation by this act with Xerxes. For it is said that the king, looking on at the battle, noticed that her ship had rammed the other; and someone present said: “Master, do you see Artemisia, how well she is fighting, and how she has just now sunk an enemy ship?” He asked whether this was truly Artemisia's deed, and they said it was — they declared they knew her ship's device very well — and that what had been destroyed must surely be one of the enemy. For besides the other things that turned out fortunately for her, as I have said, there was this too: not one of the Calyndian ship's crew survived to become her accuser. And Xerxes, in reply to what was said to him, is reported to have uttered these words: “My men have become women, and my women, men.” So, it is said, Xerxes spoke.
